opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that concept erasure is supposed to be a surgical intervention. You want to remove one specific piece of information, say gender or part-of-speech, from a model's representations, so that no linear classifier can recover it anymore. But there are trivially many ways to do that. You could zero out the whole representation and you'd have perfectly erased the concept, but you'd also have destroyed everything else the network knows. That's obviously useless.

So the reason minimality matters is twofold. One is practical. If you're using erasure for fairness, say making sure a classifier isn't relying on a protected attribute, you want to keep as much of the model's performance as you can. Every unnecessary change you make costs you accuracy on the stuff you actually care about.

The second reason, which I find more interesting scientifically, is interpretability. A lot of the time we use erasure as a kind of causal probe: if I remove the model's access to concept X and its behavior changes in some way, that tells me the model was using X. But that inference only works if the intervention is clean. If my erasure method also scrambles a bunch of unrelated features, then when performance drops I can't tell whether it's because the model needed the concept or because I just broke the representation as collateral damage. So you want the smallest possible edit, in our case measured by expected squared distance, so that whatever effects you see can be attributed to the concept itself and not to side effects.

That's what motivated LEACE, LEAst-squares Concept Erasure. We showed there's a closed-form solution that provably guarantees no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor at recovering the concept, while moving the representations as little as possible in a least-squares sense. Earlier methods like iterative nullspace projection would often remove way more than necessary, sometimes many dimensions, and that makes the downstream conclusions much murkier. Having the minimal edit gives you a much cleaner experimental tool.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes erasing the concept so no linear classifier can recover it from minimizing representation changes, noting that many edits can achieve erasure but some destroy unrelated information.

r002.rationale: It says unnecessary changes can cost accuracy, but does not explain that this risk arises because SGD optimized the representation for the task.

r003.rationale: It mentions LEACE and part-of-speech as an example, but does not propose removing linearly available part-of-speech information at every layer during the forward pass.

r004.rationale: It explains that collateral changes make it unclear whether a behavior change came from the erased concept or from damage to unrelated features.

r005.rationale: It does not report next-token prediction loss increasing after part-of-speech erasure.

r006.rationale: It does not report that models remain above the unigram-entropy baseline after part-of-speech erasure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the whole motivation for concept erasure, at least the way I think about it, is that you want to remove one specific thing, like gender, or some sensitive attribute, or some concept you're trying to study, and leave everything else intact. And the problem is that it's very easy to "erase" a concept if you're allowed to just destroy the representation. I could zero out all the activations and now there's no gender information in there, but there's also no information about anything, so that's useless.

So the interesting version of the problem is really a constrained one. You want a transformation that makes the concept unrecoverable, in our case provably unrecoverable by any linear classifier, but which is as close to the identity as possible. That's exactly what LEACE is doing. We derive the minimal, in a least-squares sense, affine transformation that guarantees linear guarding. And the "minimal" part is doing a lot of the work, because that's what gives you the right to interpret your results afterward.

If I erase a concept and then go measure how the model's behavior changes, I want to be able to attribute that change to the concept I removed, not to collateral damage. If the surgery is sloppy and I've also wiped out a bunch of unrelated features, then any downstream effect I see is confounded. Was it because the model lost access to gender, or because I accidentally broke syntax? You can't tell. So minimality is kind of the thing that makes the counterfactual clean.

There's also a more practical angle. If you're applying this inside a model at every layer during inference, which is one of the things we do, then every bit of unnecessary distortion compounds. A small perturbation at layer five becomes a big one by layer thirty. So if you want the model to keep working, you really need each intervention to be as surgical as possible. In the experiments we actually find you can erase a concept like part-of-speech at every layer and the language modeling loss only goes up a little bit, and that's only possible because the edit is so small.

And honestly, I think there's an interpretability principle here too. A lot of the time we want to use erasure as a tool to ask, "what does the model actually use this concept for?" The answer to that question is only meaningful if you've removed just that concept and nothing else. So minimal change isn't a nice-to-have, it's kind of the whole point.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes making the concept unrecoverable by linear classifiers from keeping the transformation as close to the identity as possible.

r002.rationale: It says unnecessary distortion can harm model performance, but does not explain that SGD optimized the representation for the task.

r003.rationale: It describes erasing part-of-speech at every layer during inference and evaluating the effect on language-modeling loss, with LEACE framed as guaranteeing linear guarding.

r004.rationale: It explains that minimal edits help attribute behavioral changes to the erased concept rather than collateral damage to unrelated features.

r005.rationale: It reports that language-modeling loss goes up only a little, not that next-token prediction loss increases substantially.

r006.rationale: It does not report whether the models outperform a unigram-entropy baseline.

astra-6.text:
Well, if all you cared about was removing information about a concept, you could just set all the activations to zero. That would certainly erase the concept, but it would also destroy everything else the network was doing. So you need some constraint that says: remove this information while preserving as much of the rest as possible.

That’s especially important if you’re using concept erasure to understand the model. You want to intervene, erase some concept, and see how its behavior changes. If your intervention also damages a bunch of unrelated information, then you can’t confidently attribute the change in behavior to the concept you intended to erase. Minimizing the change to the representation helps make that experiment more informative, although it doesn’t by itself guarantee that the intervention is perfectly selective.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts erasing a concept with preserving other information, but does not distinguish linear guardedness from minimizing representational change.

r002.rationale: It says erasure could destroy other network behavior, but does not explain that changing the representation risks task performance because SGD optimized it for the task.

r003.rationale: It does not propose testing part-of-speech dependence with LEACE applied at every layer during the forward pass.

r004.rationale: It explains that changing unrelated information makes behavioral changes hard to attribute to the erased concept, and that minimizing representational change makes the experiment more informative.

r005.rationale: It reports no next-token prediction loss result for erasing linearly available part-of-speech information.

r006.rationale: It does not report whether the models outperform a unigram-entropy baseline after erasure.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you want to isolate the effect of that concept. If you erase gender information, say, but also destroy a bunch of unrelated information, then a change in the model’s behavior doesn’t tell you very much. Was it caused by removing gender, or by all the other damage you did?

So changing the representation as little as possible gives you a cleaner intervention. You’re trying to remove the information you care about while preserving everything else, both so the model remains useful and so you can interpret what happens afterward. Of course, “as little as possible” depends on how you measure distance, so that’s an assumption you have to make explicit.

r001.rationale: It argues for minimal representation change but does not distinguish that goal from achieving linear guardedness.

r002.rationale: It says unrelated damage may reduce usefulness, but does not explain that SGD optimized the representation for the task or connect alteration to task performance.

r003.rationale: It proposes no test involving LEACE or removing part-of-speech information during the forward pass.

r004.rationale: It says minimizing other changes creates a cleaner intervention, helping isolate whether the concept caused a behavioral change.

r005.rationale: It reports no next-token prediction loss result.

r006.rationale: It reports no comparison with a unigram-entropy baseline.
